definition: Calibrate means to adjust precisely against a known standard.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word calibrate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know calibrate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Divers calibrate their depth gauges against the pool's marked ten-meter line before any open-water trip.
Adjust is far looser than calibrate — turn it until it seems right, with nothing to answer to, while calibrating must answer to a known standard.
Fine-tune stops short of calibrate — the touches are small and careful, but only calibrating checks them against a known standard.

Align means to bring things into agreement or into line with each other — two schedules, a policy and a mission, a wheel and an axle. Calibrate is narrower and more exacting: to calibrate is to true one instrument against a known standard, and the job ends only when the two agree.

Standardize means to make many things match one agreed norm — forms, sizes, procedures across a whole system. Calibrate works on one instrument at a time: you calibrate a scale against a known standard until it reads true. Standardizing writes the rule; calibrating brings a single tool into line with it.

We still call a leader 'of high caliber' — the old word for a barrel's exact measure, turned into a measure of quality.
Calibrate means to adjust precisely against a known standard.
On the first Monday of each month, the pharmacist sets a certified brass weight — exactly one hundred grams, sealed and stamped — on the dispensary scale.
If the display strays by even a tenth of a gram, she calibrates the instrument, working the adjustment screw until scale and weight agree, then hangs the brass back in its case until next month.
Calibrate is the exact word for that monthly ritual, because calibrate means to adjust precisely against a known standard — the stamped weight is the standard, and the scale is bent to match it.
Adjust alone covers any nudge in any direction; calibrating requires something true to aim at, and it ends only when the instrument agrees with the truth.
Calibrate is bench language — instruments, sensors, scales — and it always implies a standard somewhere in the room.
Adjust covers every looser case; fine-tune sits between.
Figuratively you can calibrate a speech to its audience, and the standard is still there: the audience is the reference the wording is trued against.

The robotics team learned about weigh-ins the hard way: last year their robot passed on their own bathroom scale and failed at the competition table by two hundred grams.
This season the team captain drives to the county inspection office every February.
There, for a small fee, she can calibrate the team's shop scale against the office's sealed reference weights — a one-kilogram cylinder certified to a tenth of a gram.
She loosens the tare screw, sets the cylinder on the plate, and works in tiny turns until the display reads 1000.0 three times in a row.
The scale never leaves the shop after that, and no robot of theirs has failed a weigh-in since.
